description: Runs cleaning stations on the reef, climbing onto visiting fish to pick off parasites and dead skin, and will even groom a diver's hand. Adults are simultaneous hermaphrodites, so any two can pair and both carry eggs, which hatch as planktonic larvae at night.

region: Tropical Atlantic — Caribbean, Brazil & eastern Atlantic islands
description: The Atlantic twin of the Pacific cleaner shrimp, told apart by its white back stripe running unbroken onto the tail fan, which lacks the Pacific species' white spots. It sets up cleaning stations in crevices and, like its relative, is a simultaneous hermaphrodite.

region: Indo-Pacific — Indian Ocean to Indonesia & the Philippines
description: A blood-red cleaner shrimp sprinkled with white spots, with white legs and antennae, that lives in pairs in caves and overhangs on deeper reef slopes. It is shyer than the skunk cleaners and does most of its foraging after dark.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida, Gulf of Mexico & Caribbean
description: A translucent shrimp candy-striped with thin red lines that reef keepers buy to eat the pest anemone Aiptasia. Groups forage at night, and unlike most marine shrimp its larvae can be raised in captivity.

region: Eastern Gulf of Mexico — west coast of Florida
description: Described only in 2006, this Florida Gulf-coast species is the peppermint shrimp most often collected for the trade and long passed as L. wurdemanni. It is a dependable eater of Aiptasia anemones and, like its relatives, its larvae have been reared in captivity.

region: Eastern Pacific — central California to Baja California
description: A temperate relative of the peppermint shrimp that crowds into rocky crevices by the hundreds and cleans fish such as moray eels. Its translucent body is lined with red stripes; it is a staple of cold-water public aquarium displays.

region: Circumtropical — Indo-Pacific, Red Sea & tropical Atlantic
description: A spiny cleaner shrimp with red-and-white banded claws and very long white antennae, usually found as a mated pair that holds the same crevice for years. Pairs are faithful to each other but fight other members of their species to the death.

A small banded coral shrimp whose carapace is a vivid blue-violet in front of a red-and-white banded abdomen and claws. Like its larger relative it lives in mated pairs in reef crevices and is intolerant of others of its kind.

The Caribbean's golden banded coral shrimp: a yellow body crossed by red bands, with red-and-white banded claws and white antennae. Pairs hold a crevice and clean passing fish, and are as intolerant of their own kind as the common banded coral shrimp.

A tiny orange-brown shrimp with blue-rimmed white saddles that sways its upturned tail almost constantly, hence its trade name. Small groups live among the tentacles of sea anemones, mushroom corals and other cnidarians.

A glass-clear Caribbean cleaner with violet-banded legs that lives among the tentacles of corkscrew and giant anemones, whipping its white antennae to advertise its services to passing fish. It is one of the most important cleaners on Caribbean reefs.

An almost transparent shrimp with a white-and-yellow V-shaped patch on its humped abdomen and white legs tipped with blue-violet. It lives on sea anemones, large-polyp corals and even jellyfish, and cleans fish that visit its host.

A glassy shrimp whose carapace and abdomen carry bands of white specks outlined in red, with a white tail and hump and pale turquoise claws that it rocks from side to side. It lives on sea anemones and large-polyp corals and cleans fish.
Lives in carpet and other large anemones, where a big female often shares the host with a much smaller male. It is named for the row of orange-ringed white eyespots along the edge of its tail fan.

A transparent shrimp with brown-and-white saddle markings and boldly purple-and-white banded legs and claws. It lives among the tentacles of Caribbean anemones and sways and waves its antennae to attract fish to clean.

Groups hover in caves and holes on the reef, beating their swimmerets to drift toward fish that come to be cleaned. The glassy body is dotted with red and yellow, with a red spot behind a white one at the sharp bend of the abdomen.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: Eats nothing but starfish: a pair flips a sea star over, drags it to their lair and feeds on it alive for days, starting with the tube feet. Its huge flattened claws and petal-like antennae are covered in blue- or purple-edged pink spots.

A stout little shrimp banded dark brown and cream like a bumblebee, with blue and orange highlights on its legs and tail. In the wild it feeds on the tube feet of sea urchins and sea stars, hiding under rubble by day.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Indonesia & Japan
description: Named for its sharply humped abdomen, this red shrimp with white-edged stripes has a hinged beak (rostrum) it can tilt up and down. Groups shelter in crevices by day and come out at night to scavenge — including zoanthid and soft-coral polyps.

A mottled green, brown and red shrimp dotted with white and fringed with tufts of setae that camouflage it on reef rubble; males grow extraordinarily long first claws. It hides deep in the rockwork by day and scavenges at night.

A white shrimp banded in red that shares a sand burrow with a goby such as Stonogobiops: the near-blind shrimp digs and maintains the tunnel while keeping an antenna on its partner, which watches for danger. Its enlarged claw snaps shut with a loud pop that stuns small prey.

A cream shrimp patterned with large, gold-rimmed dark blotches that pairs with watchman gobies such as Cryptocentrus and Amblyeleotris, digging the shared burrow while the goby stands guard. Like all pistol shrimp it stuns prey with a bubble shot from its snapping claw.

A yellow-orange pistol shrimp with purple legs and claws and a large deep-red spot ringed in white on each side of the body — the 'bullseye'. It lives hidden in rubble and crevices and stuns small prey with a snap of its enlarged claw.

A brilliantly coloured 'smasher' whose club-like raptorial appendages strike fast enough to form cavitation bubbles, shattering snail and crab shells — and occasionally aquarium glass. Its stalked eyes carry about a dozen kinds of colour receptor, and it lives in a U-shaped burrow in rubble.
The largest mantis shrimp, a 'spearer' that waits at the mouth of a deep vertical burrow in sand and impales passing fish with barbed raptorial claws. Its pale body is crossed by dark zebra bands.
A small, flattened green crab with hairy legs and spoon-tipped claws, stocked in reef tanks to pick off bubble algae (Valonia). It wedges itself into rock crevices by day and forages mostly at night.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & North Carolina to Brazil
description: A small red cousin of the emerald crab whose carapace is sculpted into raised ridges, with spoon-tipped claws and hairy legs. It hides deep in rock crevices and grazes algae and detritus at night.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida, Gulf of Mexico & Caribbean
description: The largest reef crab of the Caribbean (formerly Mithrax spinosissimus), a spiny reddish-brown spider crab that eats chemically defended and calcified algae other grazers avoid. It is being farmed and released to clear algae from Caribbean reefs and suits only large public displays.

A spotted porcelain crab that lives in pairs among the tentacles of carpet anemones, sweeping the water with feathery mouthparts to catch plankton. Though crab-shaped it is closer to the squat lobsters, and like other porcelain crabs it readily drops a leg to escape.

Carries a tiny sea anemone in each claw and waves them at intruders like boxing gloves or pom-poms; the anemones also snare food, which the crab steals from them. Its pink-and-yellow shell is tessellated with dark-outlined polygons.

Hawaii's own boxer crab, barely over a centimetre across, which carries a small anemone in each claw for defence and food gathering. Its shell is patterned with pink, brown and yellow polygons and its legs are banded dark purple, making it almost invisible on rubble.

Lives only among the branches of Pocillopora corals, which give it shelter and nutritious mucus; in return the crab defends its host by pinching the tube feet of coral-eating crown-of-thorns starfish. Its smooth cream shell is covered with red-orange spots.

region: Tropical Atlantic & eastern Pacific; invasive in the Mediterranean
description: An extremely flat crab (also called the nimble spray crab) with long gold-ringed legs that skitters sideways over surge-swept rocks grazing algae. Native to both sides of the tropical Atlantic and the eastern Pacific, it has spread through the Mediterranean since the late 1990s.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina to Brazil
description: A spindly spider crab with a long pointed rostrum, a triangular body striped gold and dark brown, and violet-tipped claws, often perched on sponges and anemones. It is kept to eat bristleworms, but large individuals also catch small shrimp and sleeping fish.

A spider crab that snips off bits of sponge, algae and debris and hooks them onto velcro-like hairs on its body and legs, becoming a walking piece of reef. It redecorates after every molt, using whatever it can find.

A small swimming crab with paddle-shaped hind legs that lives commensally on tube anemones (Cerianthus) and Actinodendron anemones. Its reddish shell is covered with large white blotches and its legs are semi-transparent white.

A rounded little swimming crab boldly patched in white and maroon-brown that lives on large sea cucumbers, sheltering on their skin and even in the mouth or cloaca. Paddle-like hind legs let it swim between hosts.

The classic Caribbean clean-up hermit, with bright blue legs banded orange-yellow and orange antennae, living in large aggregations on shallow rubble. It grazes film algae and scavenges leftovers, and competes with snails for shells.

The red-legged hermit of the Gulf of California, with red to red-brown legs and claws and red antennae. Hardy and tolerant, it is sold in reef clean-up crews to eat film algae and detritus, though it will also take snails for their shells.

A large hermit of seagrass beds, oyster reefs and mud flats, recognised by thin pale stripes running lengthwise down its olive-brown legs. It is a powerful scavenger that will kill snails for food or shells, so it suits only robust tanks.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii
description: An intertidal reef-flat hermit whose left claw is far larger than the right and plugs the shell opening when it withdraws. Its purplish-brown claws have white fingertips and its eyestalks are blue at the base and orange at the tip; it fights readily over shells.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & French Polynesia
description: Its walking legs are ringed in alternating electric blue and black, its claws olive-green speckled with white, and its antennae orange; Hawaiian animals often show orange instead of blue bands. It lives on shallow reef flats and rubble, grazing algae and scavenging.

A small, entirely scarlet Caribbean hermit with bright yellow eyestalks that lives on reefs rather than on shallow flats. It is among the gentlest clean-up hermits and grazes hair algae, cyanobacteria and detritus.

A huge hermit, red-orange and covered with black-edged white spots and stiff bristles, that moves into ever larger shells such as tritons and big turbans. It is a voracious scavenger and predator that will eat snails, crabs and sleeping fish.

Plants sea anemones (Calliactis polypus) on its shell for protection, coaxing each one off the rock by tapping and massaging its base and carrying it along to every new shell. It has short red-and-white banded eyestalks and large pinkish claws.

The most brightly coloured hermit in the hobby, with red legs striped lengthwise in orange-yellow and dark-tipped pincers. Its flattened body and claws let it use narrow-mouthed shells such as cones; it is more scavenger than algae eater.

region: Gulf of California & Pacific coast of Mexico
description: A heavy turban snail prized for mowing down hair algae; its rounded shell is mottled green-brown with dark wavy bands. Like other turbans it seals its shell with a thick, chalky operculum when disturbed.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina to Brazil, Gulf of Mexico & Caribbean
description: A small turban with spiral rows of beads, tan to light brown with patches of reddish-brown and cream (some are all orange). It grazes film algae and diatoms on rubble and seagrass beds.

The cone-shaped 'Astraea' of reef clean-up crews, a Caribbean grazer of film algae and diatoms on rock and glass. Its tall, ribbed pyramid shell is often overgrown with algae, and if it lands on its back it frequently cannot right itself.

A small, strongly ribbed star shell, white to greenish and often fouled with algae, that grazes diatoms and film algae. It is sold alongside the larger Astraea snail and shares its trouble righting itself when knocked over.
A conical top shell with beaded spiral ribs mottled red, green and cream, grazing film algae from glass and rock. Unlike turbans it can flip itself upright, and it often spawns in reef tanks.

region: Central & western Pacific — Indo-Malaysia to New Caledonia
description: A solid, pyramid-shaped top shell with thick oblique ribs, white to grey mottled with green, brown or olive over a plain white base; the foot is white with fine black dots. Sold as the 'Tectus' or 'Trochus' snail, it grazes film algae and can right itself if flipped.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina to Brazil & Gulf of Mexico
description: A slender, tall-spired snail of seagrass beds and rubble, whitish with rows of dark brown beads and spots. It grazes diatoms, film algae and detritus, burrows into sand at times, and its egg strings on the glass often hatch in reef tanks.
A stout cerith with a row of blunt knobs on each whorl, white with neat spiral rows of square black spots, as if lettered. It grazes film algae and detritus in shallow rubble and seagrass.

region: Western Atlantic — Cape Cod to Brazil
description: A small, thick-shelled mud snail that lies buried with only its siphon showing, then erupts from the sand within seconds of food hitting the water. It keeps sand beds stirred and cleans up uneaten food and carrion.

A larger nassarius with a smooth, polished cream shell banded in rose, which spends most of its time buried with only a long siphon above the sand. It scavenges carrion and leftovers and ploughs through the sand bed as it goes.

A small conch named for the strawberry-red mouth of its shell, edged in black; the outside is cream streaked with orange-brown. It ploughs over sand grazing film algae and detritus, peering out on long eyestalks, and can leap away using its sickle-shaped operculum.

A sturdy chestnut to orange-brown conch (sometimes treated as Strombus pugilis alatus) with short spines on the shoulders and a salmon-coloured aperture. It sifts sand for diatoms and detritus and moves in jerky vaults by planting its sickle-shaped operculum.

The Caribbean's iconic conch (long known as Strombus or Lobatus gigas), with a heavy knobbed spire, a flaring lip and a glossy pink aperture. It grazes algae and detritus on seagrass and sand; overfishing means aquarium animals are hatchery-reared juveniles.

A heavy conch whose flared lip bears six long, curved finger-like spines; the outside is mottled brown and cream and the aperture glossy pink-orange. It grazes algae and detritus on reef flats and seagrass beds.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: A large cowrie whose glossy white shell is heavily spotted in dark brown; at night it wraps the shell in a brown mantle studded with white-tipped papillae, which keeps the gloss polished. It grazes algae and sponges and may nibble soft corals.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Polynesia
description: Named for the dense brown markings on its glossy back that look like Arabic script, over a fawn and bluish-grey ground with dark-spotted margins. It shelters in crevices by day and grazes algae at night.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Galápagos
description: A small, flattened cowrie with a pale yellow shell and thick, knobby margins, used as currency across Africa and Asia for centuries. It lives on shallow reef flats and grazes algae.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Polynesia
description: A small cowrie whose grey-blue to white back is encircled by a bright golden ring, also once traded as shell money. It grazes algae on rock and rubble on shallow reef flats.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & Caribbean to Brazil
description: A large, elongate cowrie, glossy brown dotted with round white spots, those low on the sides with dark centres. It hides under ledges by day and grazes algae at night.

An elongate, ear-shaped abalone whose olive-and-brown shell is too small to cover its large green-and-brown foot; it breathes through a row of open holes along the shell edge. It grazes algae at night and clamps hard to rock by day.

A small abalone with a variably mottled shell — green, brown, cream or red — that often arrives as a hitchhiker on live rock. It hides under rocks by day and grazes film algae at night, breathing through a row of shell holes.

A fast little snail with a flattened, ear-shaped shell too small to withdraw into; when grabbed it sheds the end of its foot like a lizard's tail. It hitchhikes in on live rock, breeds freely in reef tanks and grazes film algae at night.

A small snail from cold Pacific shores, its spiral-ridged grey-tan shell showing pearly nacre where worn. Widely sold as a reef-tank grazer, it is a cold-water animal and rarely lives long at tropical temperatures.

An intertidal Caribbean nerite whose rounded white shell is painted with spiral rows of black and red dashes; the aperture bears four teeth. It grazes film algae on rock and glass and often climbs out above the waterline.

A small, flat sea star with five rounded arms, red to orange with tiny dark pores scattered over its granular surface. It feeds on biofilm, detritus and microalgae and is one of the few sea stars that suit an established reef tank.

Its red-orange skin is set with rows of pale cream plates like tiles, ending in solid red arm tips; it is also sold as the peppermint or necklace sea star. It grazes biofilm and detritus and does well in mature reef tanks if acclimated slowly.

A deep red to orange sea star marbled with paler cream and tipped with black or dark brown on all five arms; some show a fine black lattice on top. It grazes biofilm and detritus and is among the better sea stars for mature reef tanks.

A brilliant blue sea star with five long, smooth, sausage-like arms, common on Indo-Pacific reef flats. It feeds on biofilm and detritus, ships poorly, and often slowly starves in anything but a large, mature system.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: A small, slender-armed linckia mottled in red, orange and purple with darker spots. It reproduces by shedding arms that regrow into new stars, so many individuals are lopsided 'comets' with one long arm.

A long-armed orange-red to brownish linckia found on reefs around the tropics, often with arms of unequal length from regeneration. Like its relatives it grazes biofilm and needs a large, mature tank.

A flat, grey-beige sea star edged with marginal spines that spends much of the day buried, ploughing through sand to eat detritus and tiny animals. At spawning time males climb onto females and stay in this 'pseudocopulation' pose for days.

A fast, flat sea star fringed with stiff comb-like marginal spines, purplish-brown along the middle of each arm with pale orange edges. It burrows in sand and swallows small snails, clams and crustaceans whole, and its tissues contain tetrodotoxin.

A stiff, five-armed sea star with a tan body studded with dark brown conical knobs like chocolate chips, common on shallow seagrass and sand flats. It will eat corals, sponges, clams and other sessile animals, so it belongs in fish-only systems.

region: Western Indian Ocean — East Africa & Madagascar
description: A grey sea star patterned with a network of bright red ridges linking red conical knobs along each arm, from shallow East African lagoons. It preys on corals, sponges, clams and even other sea stars, so it suits only fish-only tanks.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bahamas to Brazil
description: A massive, thick-bodied sea star whose upper surface is a raised net of knobs, orange-red to tan in adults and mottled olive-green in juveniles. It roams seagrass and sand flats, turning its stomach out over sediment films, sponges and detritus.

An inflated, nearly armless sea star shaped like a pentagonal pillow, mottled tan, orange, green or red. It feeds largely on live coral by everting its stomach over the colony, so it is unsuitable for reef tanks.

A plump sea star with short, finger-like arms and smooth granular skin, pinkish-tan to orange with darker red arm tips. It scavenges detritus and biofilm but may also feed on sessile invertebrates, so it is best kept away from corals.

A tiny, often lopsided sea star — usually with six or seven unequal arms — that arrives on live rock and multiplies by splitting in two. Most graze film algae and detritus on glass and rock, but some populations nibble zoanthids and Acropora.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida, Gulf of Mexico & Caribbean
description: A slender-armed sea star, red-orange to brick-brown and rough with rows of short conical spines, found in seagrass beds, bays and rubble. It feeds on detritus, biofilm and small encrusting invertebrates.

region: Northeastern Pacific — Alaska to Baja California
description: The keystone predator of Pacific rocky shores, prying mussels apart with its tube feet; Robert Paine's removal experiments with it founded the keystone-species concept. Purple or orange with a lacy net of white spines, it was hit hard by sea star wasting disease from 2013.

region: Northeastern Pacific — Alaska to Baja California
description: A webbed, short-armed sea star of Pacific kelp forests and rocky shores, coloured anything from red, orange and yellow to purple, often mottled. It scavenges by turning its stomach out over algae, detritus and dead animals, and is a fixture of aquarium touch pools.

A big, bright green brittle star with banded arms that hides under rock with only its arm tips showing, then pins and eats small fish, shrimp and anything else it can catch. A fine scavenger alongside large fish, it is a known killer of gobies and other small tankmates.

region: Indo-West Pacific — western Indian Ocean to New Caledonia
description: A beige to yellow-orange brittle star with bold purple-black bands across its arms and a variably patterned disc, living under coral rubble on shallow reefs. It is a shy, harmless scavenger of detritus and leftover food.

A uniformly black brittle star bristling with stout arm spines, readily told from its relatives by its bright red tube feet. It hides under rocks and dead coral by day and sweeps its arms over the bottom for detritus at night.

A smooth, solid scarlet serpent star whose scale-covered arms lack the bristling spines of most other brittle stars. A hardy scavenger, it snakes its arms toward food as soon as any reaches the bottom.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: A smooth-armed serpent star with grey arms ringed by pale bands and a grey, brown or white disc that is often spotted. It lives under rocks and coral rubble and scavenges detritus and leftovers at night.
A large, smooth-armed serpent star of Caribbean outer reefs, ruby red with narrow cream bands along its arms. It shelters in crevices by day and forages over the reef at night.

The tiny six-armed brittle star that colonises almost every reef tank, hitching in on live rock and multiplying by splitting across the disc. Mottled green and tan with banded arms, it hides in rock and sponge crevices and harmlessly scavenges detritus.

A small, round urchin whose test has ten bare blue-green bands between tracts of short dark spines, like a dinner jacket. It grazes film and coralline algae and often carries bits of shell or rubble on top for shade and camouflage.

A pale, round-tested urchin covered in short spines banded green and maroon (or white and maroon), common in seagrass beds and on muddy sand. It grazes algae, bryozoans and detritus and often carries shells and debris for cover.

A black urchin with hollow, needle-sharp spines up to 30 cm long that snap off in skin, recognised by five white spots on the test and a bright orange ring around the anal cone. It hides in crevices by day and grazes algae at night, and small fish shelter among its spines.

Very like Diadema setosum but lacking the orange anal ring; instead its dark test is marked with brilliant iridescent blue lines. It shelters in groups in crevices by day and comes out to graze algae at night.

region: Tropical western Atlantic — Florida & Bermuda to Brazil
description: Once the Caribbean's dominant algae grazer, this black, long-spined urchin was all but wiped out by a disease in 1983–84, after which many reefs became choked with seaweed. Hatchery-reared animals are now released to help restore reefs.

A large diadematid with two kinds of spine: long, thick primaries often banded brown and white, and short, fine venomous secondaries; a big bronze anal sac speckled with white sits on top. It shelters in crevices by day and grazes algae at night.

A large, flattened urchin with a red-brown test marked by five V-shaped rows of iridescent blue dots and long, banded venomous spines. It roams open sand and rubble with juvenile fish and shrimp sheltering among its spines, and small ones are sometimes carried about on the backs of carrier crabs.

An oval-tested urchin that grinds a burrow into reef rock with its spines and teeth and may stay in it for life. Its spines vary from green to purple or brown, each with a pale ring at the base; it grazes drift and turf algae near its hole.

region: Tropical Atlantic — Florida & Caribbean to Brazil, and West Africa
description: A common shallow-water urchin of the tropical Atlantic, oval and black to reddish-brown, that bores cup-shaped hollows into intertidal and shallow reef rock. It stays in its burrow by day and grazes drift algae trapped by its spines.

Named for its thick, blunt primary spines, once used as pencils for writing on slates; they are red-brown with pale rings. It wedges itself into surge-zone crevices by day and grazes coralline and turf algae at night, but may also eat sessile invertebrates.

A big, short-spined urchin that heaps shells and algae fragments on its back, which gives it its name. A voracious grazer of macroalgae, it is hatchery-reared in Hawaii and released to clear invasive seaweeds from reefs.

region: Tropical Atlantic — Florida & Caribbean to Brazil, and West Africa
description: A large urchin with a dark test densely covered in short white spines, grazing turtle grass and algae on shallow seagrass beds. It is harvested for its roe in parts of the Caribbean, where overfishing has depleted some populations.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil
description: A short-spined urchin, green, white, purple or red, that covers itself with seagrass blades and shell fragments as it grazes seagrass and algae. It is also a classic model animal in developmental biology.
A small urchin with deep green or white spines and conspicuous purple pedicellariae and tube feet between them, giving it a jewelled look. It hides under rubble by day and grazes film and turf algae.

region: Tropical Atlantic — North Carolina to Brazil, and West Africa
description: A cidarid urchin with a few thick, blunt primary spines, often encrusted with algae and sponges, set on a red-brown test. It hides in crevices by day and at night eats coralline algae, sponges, carrion and sometimes corals.

region: Northeastern Pacific — British Columbia to Baja California
description: The purple urchin of Pacific rocky shores, which scrapes pits into rock and, when predators such as sea otters and sunflower stars decline, multiplies into 'urchin barrens' that strip kelp forests. Individuals can live for decades.
